title: Producer Consumer
body:
The classic [[Synchronization]] problem, and the shape of most real concurrent code. One or
more **producers** make items and put them in a shared buffer; one or more **consumers**
take items out and use them. They run at different, unpredictable speeds.

The three things that must never happen:

1. A consumer takes from an empty buffer.
2. A producer writes into a full buffer.
3. Both touch the buffer at the same instant and corrupt it.

Note that these are two different kinds of requirement. (3) is
[[Mutual Exclusion]] over the [[Critical Section]]. (1) and (2) are *counting*: you have to
know how many items and how many free slots there are, which plain
[[Mutex Lock|mutual exclusion]] cannot tell you. That is why the solution needs
[[Semaphores]] and not just a lock, and it is the best argument in the course for
semaphores existing at all.

## The solution

[[Bounded Buffer Problem]] owns the code and the three semaphores (`mutex`, `slot_avail`,
`item_avail`) with their initial values. Read that note for the mechanism; this one is the
problem statement.

The short version: `mutex` at 1 handles requirement (3), `slot_avail` counting down from
*n* handles (2), `item_avail` counting up from 0 handles (1). Producer waits on
`slot_avail`, consumer waits on `item_avail`, and each posts the other's semaphore on the
way out.

**Order matters.** Take the `mutex` before the counting semaphore rather than after and you
can end up holding the lock while blocking on a buffer that only the other side can unblock,
which nothing will ever resolve.

## Where you have already seen it

- [[Piping]]: `ls | grep` is a producer and a consumer with a kernel buffer between them,
  and the blocking is the kernel enforcing exactly these rules.
- [[Buffering]] and [[Double Buffering]] from [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]]: the device is the
  producer, your program is the consumer, and an [[Interrupts|interrupt]] is the signal.
- Any work queue: threads pushing jobs, a pool of workers popping them.
